key_big: Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent.
key_sub: A pure substance melts at one fixed temperature.
body_html:
How to think about it

Chemists test whether a substance is pure and what is in it.

  • A pure substance melts and boils at fixed temperatures; a mixture melts over a range.
  • Chromatography: Rf = spot distance ÷ solvent distance. Spots at the same height are the same dye.
  • Gas tests: hydrogen pops, oxygen relights a glowing splint, carbon dioxide turns limewater milky, chlorine bleaches damp litmus.
Example

Spot 3 cm, solvent 6 cm. Rf?

3 ÷ 6

Answer: 0.5

Example

Glowing splint relights. Gas?

The oxygen test

Answer: oxygen

Common mistakes

  • Thinking 'pure' means 'natural'.
  • Dividing the solvent distance by the spot distance.
  • Mixing up the oxygen and hydrogen tests.

faq.q: How do you calculate an Rf value?
faq.a: Divide the distance moved by the spot by the distance moved by the solvent, both measured from the start line. Rf is always less than 1.

faq.q: How can you tell if a substance is pure?
faq.a: A pure substance melts at one exact temperature. An impure substance melts at a lower temperature over a range.

faq.q: What are the four gas tests?
faq.a: Hydrogen: squeaky pop with a lit splint. Oxygen: relights a glowing splint. Carbon dioxide: limewater turns milky. Chlorine: bleaches damp litmus paper.
